questions.explanation: Users intuitively sense organizing logic; signage supports but doesn't replace geometric clarity. Principles directly affect spatial experience. Principles organize interior spaces as much as exterior forms. Organizing principles are fundamental to how people understand and move through buildings. A clear centralized principle (find the center, then find your destination) aids wayfinding. A linear principle (follow the spine) creates clear procession. questions.explanation: Radial employs radial geometry; centralized can too. Geometry doesn't distinguish them. Both appear in sacred and secular contexts. Both can have multiple axes depending on complexity. Critical distinction: centralized clusters forms around a center without radiating arms (like a dome surrounded by chapels—compact, inward). Radial has arms extending outward from core (like Washington D.C. avenues radiating from Capitol—expansive, reaching). Both have centers, but opposite spatial characters. questions.explanation: Both are intentionally planned; neither is ad hoc. Both grid and clustered offer more flexibility than linear, which needs directional extension. Grid is actually quite flexible within its modular discipline. questions.explanation: Centralized depends on the importance of the center; additions challenge that hierarchy. Linear can extend but only in predictable directions. Radial can add spokes but within the hub-and-spoke logic. Clustered organization is inherently flexible—new buildings can be added to a cluster without restructuring the whole (unlike linear, which needs extension direction, or centralized, which competes with center).
